item.title: I swapped TrueNAS for Debian and Cockpit on my 8GB home server, and got 2.5GB of RAM back
item.itunes:title: I swapped TrueNAS for Debian and Cockpit on my 8GB home server, and got 2.5GB of RAM back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Everyone told me a NAS needs a NAS OS, and for years I believed it. TrueNAS 25.10 ran my home server, and plenty of people keep coming back to it for good reasons. Then I looked at my dashboard and saw 3.2GB of my 8GB of RAM gone before a single file moved.

With RAM this expensive, buying one of the best NAS boxes felt like the wrong fix. So I installed plain Debian 13 and added Cockpit, the browser dashboard for Linux servers. Three weeks in, it's doing more with less, and I'm not going back.

TrueNAS wanted 8GB just to run itself

The math wasn't mathing

TrueNAS isn't heavy by accident. Its own hardware guide asks for 8GB of RAM as the baseline, because the middleware, the web UI, the apps system, and ZFS all share one pool of memory. On my repurposed desktop with two 4TB WD Red Plus drives in a mirror, that left ZFS little room for its read cache, which is what makes a NAS feel fast. Every time I opened the dashboard, that memory bar made me a little grumpy.

I'm not the only one who noticed. A colleague who tested TrueNAS against Unraid and ZimaOS called that 8GB floor a pretty high number in the middle of the RAM apocalypse, and I felt that in my wallet.

The other wall was apt. TrueNAS is built on Debian, but try to install a package from the shell, and you get a flat refusal: "Package management tools are disabled on TrueNAS appliances". I get why, since it's an appliance and iXsystems doesn't want people breaking it and then filing bug reports. Still, I just wanted restic for off-site backups, and the answer was always to wrap it in an app.

I tested TrueNAS, Unraid, and OpenMediaVault to find the perfect NAS OS, and there's a clear winner

Each distro has its perks and quirks

24
By  Ayush Pande

How to move a TrueNAS ZFS pool to Debian with Cockpit

The scary part was one command

I saved the TrueNAS config file, exported the pool, and installed Debian 13 with no desktop, just SSH and the standard system utilities. ZFS lives in Debian's contrib repo, and trixie-backports currently carries OpenZFS 2.4.3, which is newer than the 2.3.4 that shipped with TrueNAS 25.10. One zpool import tank later, my 3.6TB of photos, work files, and Linux ISOs I swear I'll use someday showed up exactly where I'd left them. I may have exhaled aloud.

Export the pool from TrueNAS before you wipe anything, and keep a copy of the config file off the server. If the move goes sideways, you can reinstall TrueNAS and import everything back.

Install Cockpit from Debian's backports to get the newest release: sudo apt install -t trixie-backports cockpit cockpit-podman cockpit-machines. The dashboard then lives at port 9090 on your server.

Cockpit itself is a one-line install, and the plugins do the NAS part. 45Drives' cockpit-file-sharing manages Samba and NFS shares (it handles iSCSI and S3, too), cockpit-podman runs containers, and cockpit-machines handles virtual machines. Rebuilding my four SMB shares and one NFS export took about 15 minutes, mostly because I renamed one share halfway through and then forgot which name I'd picked.

If you're turning an old PC into a NAS from scratch, this is the same flow minus the import. You pick the drives, build the pool, and share it from the browser.

Cockpit vs. TrueNAS memory use on the same hardware

Socket activation does the heavy lifting

The trick is that Cockpit barely runs. It starts on demand through socket activation, so when nobody's logged in to the dashboard, it isn't running at all. Everything it shows is the real system, meaning the same services, logs, disks, and containers I'd touch from the terminal. Close the tab, and the server goes back to being a quiet Debian box.

TrueNAS 25.10

Debian 13 + Cockpit

System RAM in use at idle (no apps)

3.2GB

640MB

Boot to SMB shares online

2 min 41 sec

52 sec

Running day to day

2 apps

3 containers + 1 VM

Install any Debian package

No

Yes

The first time I opened Cockpit's Overview page after the switch, the memory graph sat so low that I assumed it was broken. I refreshed it three times, then checked free -h in the terminal just to be sure. It wasn't broken. That's just what an idle Debian server looks like.

That freed memory went straight to work. Jellyfin, Syncthing, and Uptime Kuma now run as Podman containers, and a 2GB Home Assistant VM lives in cockpit-machines. On TrueNAS, running that VM alongside two apps pushed the box into swap. Here, ZFS still gets about 3.4GB for its cache with everything running.

Even the boring jobs moved into the browser. Since Cockpit 356, the Services page can create systemd timers that run shell commands, so my nightly snapshot and the restic backup to a friend's server are two timers I can edit without opening a terminal.

My Mac's backups were the one thing that broke

And it wasn't Cockpit's fault

Two days in, my MacBook Air M2 stopped seeing its Time Machine share. TrueNAS had quietly been setting up Apple's extras for me, and plain Samba doesn't. The share needed vfs objects = fruit streams_xattr and fruit:time machine = yes, and the server needed avahi-daemon so the Mac could find it on the network. cockpit-file-sharing has an advanced settings box for exactly this, so the fix took five minutes once I knew. Figuring that out turned into a whole evening's side quest.

That's the real catch. TrueNAS has polish I didn't notice until it was gone, like snapshot tasks, replication, and alerts that email you before a drive dies. Debian does ship a monthly ZFS scrub out of the box, but alerts are on you. I set up smartd and the ZFS event daemon to email me, and it works, but nobody's holding my hand anymore. If the box breaks at 2 a.m., the support team is me.

So if you want an appliance, TrueNAS is still the right call, and even a home lab built around VMs has better options like Proxmox. Plain Linux suits a small box that does a bit of everything, and for my box, the trade paid off in the first week.

Plain Linux was the NAS OS I needed

I expected to miss TrueNAS more than I do. That 3.2GB idle number that started all this is now 640MB, and the box I almost replaced runs more than it ever has. Scrolling the photo library from my phone feels snappier, too, since ZFS finally has room to cache.

If you're comfortable in a terminal and your NAS lives on modest hardware, plain Debian with Cockpit is worth a weekend. Just set up Time Machine before your Mac notices.

item.title: Google just silently raised the price for the Pixel 10a by $100, just over half a year after release
item.itunes:title: Google just silently raised the price for the Pixel 10a by $100, just over half a year after release
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Google quietly raised Pixel 10a prices by $100: 128GB now $599, 256GB $699.
  • No official notice from Google; price hike likely tied to the ongoing RAM supply crisis.
  • The new base price pushes Pixel 10a into mid-range territory against rivals like Samsung A57 5G.

It hasn't been a great few years for purchasing hardware. With the RAM crisis continuing, we've seen price hikes on everything from handheld game consoles to SBCs. Even the once-affordable Raspberry Pi got a price increase due to events getting "unsustainable."

Now, Google has upped the cost of its Pixel 10a by $100 for both its 128GB and 256GB on its official store. While the company hasn't officially released a statement explaining why, it's highly likely that the current RAM crisis is to blame.

The base Google Pixel 10a is now $599 for 128GB of storage

It's $100 more than its original release pricing

Credit: Google

As spotted by Notebookcheck, the Google Pixel 10a has undergone a stealth price hike. Back when the phone was released in March of this year, the 128GB version sold for $499 and the 256GB for $599. Now, they sell for $599 and $699, respectively. Notebookcheck points out that this puts the Google Pixel 10a's base model firmly in the mid-range pricing category, going toe-to-toe with the ever-popular Samsung Galaxy A57 5G.

Google itself has not announced the price hike or why it decided to make the change, but it's highly likely that it's due to the ongoing RAM crisis that has caused so many price increases over the past two years. It feels especially likely given how the price increase happened only seven months after the phone was released.

If you do decide to pick up a Google Pixel for yourself, it's worth going over some of the tips and tricks surrounding your new phone. For instance, one of our editors, Patrick O'Rourke, immediately disables these features on his Google Pixel whenever he gets one.

4 reasons the Pixel 10a is the only mid-range phone I recommend

Google's latest mid-range offering is by far the best smartphone for most people.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: I ignored Obsidian's graph view for years, and it turns out I was looking at the wrong graph
item.itunes:title: I ignored Obsidian's graph view for years, and it turns out I was looking at the wrong graph
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Obsidian's graph view is probably the most satisfying part of the app. If you have hundreds or thousands of notes, opening it gives you a really cool-looking interconnected web of dots, and everything is clickable. This graph view also seems to be a core part of second brain setups, and it can make any folder of markdown look a lot cleaner than it is. But getting something out of it is a different story - most people just zoom around for a bit before closing the tab.

This used to be me as well, until I realized I'd been trying to utilize the wrong graph view. Turns out, that one's the global graph view, and there's another one called the local graph view. We won't go into how long it took me to figure this out (because that's just a little embarrassing), but if you've been trying to figure out how the graph view could possibly be useful, you might also have been looking at the wrong one.

I replaced Notion, Google Tasks, and Figma with one Obsidian setup, and now I can’t go back

I built my perfect productivity hub

1
By  Parth Shah

What Obsidian's global graph view actually shows you

Turns out the graph view everyone knows is not all that

The global graph is the one most people mean when they talk about graph view. It's a core plugin that maps every note in your vault automatically, with each circle standing in for a note and lines drawn between any two that link to each other. Circles get bigger as more notes link to them. There's a button for it in the ribbon, or you can use the shortcut Ctrl + G.

Hovering over a dot shows what it's connected to before you click through to the note. The settings panel has a fair bit in it (filters, color groups, display options, plus forces that control how tightly everything clusters), and there's a time-lapse animation that adds your notes back in the order you created them.

Now, this isn't useless, it does give you the big picture. But it becomes easy to lose interest, especially if you have a sizable vault with loads of nodes and connections; it just turns into a digital hairball at that point. It shows me that two notes connect without telling me why, or what either of them has to do with whatever I'm working on. I'd reckon that any vault with 10k+ files just isn't very practical to navigate this way.

Months into Obsidian, I finally discovered features I should've used from day one

Powerful features were hiding in plain sight

By  Patrick Hearn

Where the local graph has been hiding this whole time

And what it does differently

I think that part of the reason the local graph doesn't get as much buzz is because you have to go digging for it, so many users probably just don't know it's there. There's no button for it in the ribbon, and while the global graph gets Ctrl + G, the local one doesn't get a shortcut at all. You have to open the command palette (Ctrl + P), type "graph", and pick Graph view: Open local graph. It's also tucked into the three-dot menu at the top of every note, which I just never bothered to check.

Once you select it, it will open in a split-view right next to whatever file you have open. Whereas the global graph shows you your whole vault, the local one only shows notes connected to the one you currently have open on the other side of the split view. My first note popped up with seven connections - I knew they were there, but it really puts it into perspective when you see it laid out visually.

It has nearly all the same settings as the global graph, plus a depth slider. At depth 1 you only see direct links, and each level above that pulls in notes linked to the ones already showing. There are also three toggles that only exist here. Incoming and outgoing links do what they say, while switching off neighbor links hides the lines between the surrounding notes so you only see the ones coming off your current note. I recommend playing around with these toggles until you find a view that makes sense for your workflow.

I turned Obsidian into a personal command center, and now I barely open separate apps

My notes, tasks, calendar, research, and writing finally live under one roof.

5
By  Patrick Hearn

What the local graph is actually good for

It helped me dig up stuff in my own vault

Once I kept my local graph within view, it made me see links I didn't pay attention to before. For example, my heuristics note's local graph pulled up a draft about productivity workflows and a daily note from July that I'd linked once and forgotten about. I don't think I'd have found either of those in the global graph.

Now, I also check the local graph before writing a new note, so I link to what's already there instead of repeating myself. The direction toggles help here. Switching off incoming links leaves only what a note builds on. That's handy for working out which notes actually feed into an article idea, for example, before I start outlining it. And the reverse works too if I want to see what leans on the note instead.

There are some rough edges. Hub notes wreck it - my by-area index at depth 1 is basically a mini global graph, since it links to almost everything in the vault. Pushing the depth past 2 lands you back in hairball territory pretty fast too.

6 Obsidian features and plugins I regret not using earlier

Obsidian features I should’ve mastered sooner

3

item.title: 4 Waze alternatives that give me Android Auto navigation without the privacy baggage
item.itunes:title: 4 Waze alternatives that give me Android Auto navigation without the privacy baggage
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Google Maps is great, and Waze is even better when I need up-to-date road-condition information. Between road reports and effective rerouting, it makes getting where I want to be exceptionally easy. But a navigation app is more than that. Whether it relies on a constant data connection or collects more information about me than I'm willing to share.

So, lately, I've been experimenting with a few alternatives. It's hard to replace Waze with a single app. Waze is popular because it works so well, especially with Android Auto. But that doesn't make the alternatives any less appealing. I was looking for apps that offered better offline navigation, gave me more control over my data, and offered features that mainstream apps didn't. Here's my experience using Organic Maps, OsmAnd, Magic Earth, and CoMaps over the last few days.

Organic Maps

Download entire cities, states, or countries instead of drawing map regions

I've written about Organic Maps a few times, and for good reason. The app is good, very good. Built on OpenStreetMap data, the app lets me download offline maps to my phone and provides turn-by-turn navigation without an internet connection. It also works with Android Auto, so you can use those offline maps in your car too.

That offline capability, and more specifically, the way it manages offline downloads, is what sells it. Unlike Google Maps, which makes you draw rectangles on a map and hope you've captured the entire region you wanted, Organic Maps lets you grab countries, states, and cities. This is, in my opinion, literally how every app should do it. The app is more flexible too. It can get me to my destination, and if I'm going for a hike, I can grab my phone and load up a GPX or KML file for trail guidance.

That makes it useful in more ways than one. There's the privacy angle too, of course. Organic Maps claims to have no trackers. It also has no ads or account requirements. On the flip side, the app offers basically no traffic information. So if you live in a city where traffic conditions matter when deciding when to head out, Organic Maps won't cut it.

Organic Maps
See at Google Play Store
I used Waze and Google Maps side by side, and one quickly became my favorite

Google Maps gets you there, but Waze warns you what's waiting

7
By  Dhruv Bhutani

OsmAnd

Detailed offline maps make it more than a Waze alternative

Like Organic Maps, OsmAnd is a particularly interesting app. It takes that same offline-first approach but gives you much more control over the actual navigation experience. The offline maps offer much more detail, and alongside turn-by-turn navigation, I found OsmAnd much better at lane guidance, showing me my speed.

OsmAnd also lets you pull in GPX tracks and excels at helping you curate a more bespoke route itinerary. While practically every mapping app lets you add in multiple points of interest for turn-by-turn navigation, I like OsmAnd's ease of access and interface.

The app also specifically focuses on keeping maps offline as much as possible, to the point that it'll constantly alert you to download a map for your local region. That may rub you the wrong way, but it wasn't an issue for me. Finally, the app strongly emphasizes privacy, supporting most navigation functions without sharing your location information. That said, many advanced functions, including Android Auto, are locked behind a subscription paywall. So, if you're looking for a free Waze replacement, this one won't cut it.

OsmAnd
See at Google Play Store

Magic Earth

Combine offline navigation with real-time road data

Many Waze and Google Maps alternatives miss essentials like live traffic information. Magic Earth is one of the few apps on this list that doesn't. It also offers features like dynamic rerouting and speed camera information, bringing the experience closer to mainstream options like Waze.

While Google Maps and Organic Maps rely on offline maps only when you are offline, Magic Earth blends the two by pulling in live traffic information on top of offline maps. This gives you reliable navigation even with spotty connectivity, while adding situational awareness through live traffic data. Yes, the app also takes a privacy-first approach and doesn't track user movements or create advertising profiles.

The app also stands out from other options with truly unique features.

While swapping out navigation voices isn't too rare, built-in activity recording and driver behavior monitoring certainly are. The former lets you record a particular route that you're taking. Meanwhile, the latter assigns you a score based on how you drive. From tailgating to fatigue monitoring, a multitude of factors let you improve your daily driving. I'm not sure if I want an app judging my driving, but it's an interesting feature.

That makes Magic Earth one of the best alternatives to Waze and Google Maps. The only caveat? Like OsmAnd, many of the best features are locked behind a paywall. And yes, that includes Android Auto. Which brings up the question: how much are you willing to pay for a little more convenience and a lot more privacy.

Magic Earth
See at Google Play Store

CoMaps

Offline navigation with Wikipedia built-in

Of all the apps here, CoMaps might be one of the most interesting. At first glance, it might look like an Organic Maps knockoff. But there's a lot more happening under the hood. To start, the open-source app uses the same OpenStreetMap data as Organic Maps, giving you solid navigation capabilities.

Yes, you can keep navigation data offline and even use the app for hiking and trail maps by importing GPX and KML files. But the app differs from alternatives because it also maintains an offline cache of Wikipedia data about key landmarks. So, if you're offline and using the app to create a navigation trail to a new city's key highlights, it won't just show you the route; it'll also give you background information about the highlights.

CoMaps
See at Google Play Store

There are plenty of Google Maps and Waze alternatives

Look, Waze and Google Maps are popular for a reason. These two apps handle navigation and live traffic exceptionally well. However, if you are looking for a more bespoke experience or a specific feature that isn't available on mainstream apps, like the aforementioned ability to cache Wikipedia blurbs, there are plenty of options to consider. While CoMaps is my favorite, any of these apps will suffice. Some apps require a subscription to unlock full functionality, but that's the price of privacy. The best part is that you can keep all these apps installed on your phone and switch between them based on the functionality you need at any given time.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While I continue building and managing my home lab, I keep a handful of browser tabs open. One shows the Proxmox dashboard for my HP ProDesk 600 G6, with the different VMs and LXCs on the mini PC. A second tab is the router's admin page, a third is Home Assistant, and a fourth is Jellyfin. Switching between these tabs is faster with keyboard shortcuts, but it can get tiring.

I wanted an interface that showed me my whole lab, the same way a dashboard app for self-hosted services would. I found the solution in the most unexpected app: Obsidian. Instead of adding yet another dashboard app, I used Obsidian with its plugin ecosystem to build my home lab’s front end. Two plugins I’d installed early on only got me halfway there. The third plugin brought everything together so I could use Obsidian as my home lab’s front end.

I use Obsidian to document my home lab and self-hosted services, here's how

There are tools built for documenting your home lab, but I love using Obsidian for it instead.

5
By  Adam Conway

item.title: Super Mario Bros. Wonder now runs natively on PC without emulation, and Nintendo probably isn't happy about it
item.itunes:title: Super Mario Bros. Wonder now runs natively on PC without emulation, and Nintendo probably isn't happy about it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Super Mario Bros. Wonder is reportedly running natively on PC at roughly 60fps using recompiled C++ and NVN-to-Vulkan layer.
  • The native port has graphical glitches and occasional frame drops, but is still impressive.
  • The project hasn't been released publicly (if and when it does drop, it's likely Nintendo won't be happy).

The retro game PC decompilation/recompilation scene continues to kick things up a notch, but this latest PC port is anything but retro (unless you consider 2023 old-school).

YouTuber Belamante has managed to get original Switch game Super Mario Bros. Wonder running at about 60fps on an RTX 3050-powered laptop without emulation, translation layers, or dynamic just-in-time (JIT) compilation. That said, the native port still has graphical glitches and occasional frame-rate drops. According to Belamante, their port uses recompiled C++ code, an NVN-to-Vulkan translation layer that talks directly to the Nvidia driver, and additional optimizations to get the platformer running smoothly on PC.

While the project isn't publicly available, Belamante says they plan to release the "recompiler, the NVN-to-Vulkan layer, and the NVN documentation" they used to create the Super Mario Bros. Wonder PC port at some point. Hopefully, it doesn't include any copyrighted files and requires players to supply their own disc image for it to work, because Nintendo's army of lawyers will definitely swiftly spring into action.

This is one of the first Switch games to get an unofficial native PC port

It's likely more native Switch ports are on the way

Even with the minor performance issues, Super Mario Bros. Wonder running natively on PC is impressive. Belmante says they plan to test their project with an integrated GPU "in the same class as the Switch's own Tegra X1" soon. It's worth mentioning that Belmante has just 458 YouTube subscribers, so to some extent, we have to take their word on the legitimacy of this port. However, it seems very legitimate.

Super Mario Bros. Wonder running on PC follows the release of Suyu (v0.0.4), an open-source fork of Switch emulator Yuzu that features a Static Recompiler Mode. This new feature can translate Nintendo Switch game code directly into a native x86 and x64 PC game. It's unclear if these projects are directly linked.

While Super Mario Bros. Wonder released for the original Switch in 2023, a Switch 2 update that adds 4K output when docked, smoother frame rates, faster loading, and more dropped a few months ago. In other retro game-related news, a native port of Halo: Combat Evolved recently released that's actually playable in a web browser.

Zelda: The Wind Waker finally gets the native PC port fans waited decades for, complete with 120fps support

The impressive port of the classic Zelda title also runs on iPhone, iPad, and macOS.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Your router is probably using your ISP's slow DNS, and you can fix it in minutes
item.itunes:title: Your router is probably using your ISP's slow DNS, and you can fix it in minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For the vast majority of people, which DNS their network uses is an afterthought, and by default, it's usually set to the one their ISP runs for them. That's not a bad thing, but most ISPs select their DNS server for ease of support if something were to go wrong with your connection, not because it's the fastest or most impervious to outages. Changing it on your devices one-by-one can take up a good chunk of your time, and it's not even possible to do so on some devices. The best course of action is to change it at the router, and it takes just a few minutes to do so.

I thought setting up custom domain names for my home lab was difficult - it’s actually simple

All you need are two self-hosted services and a little bit of patience

6
By  Ayush Pande

Your router picks your DNS server

You never got a say when the initial setup happened

Every time a device on your network opens a site, it first asks a DNS resolver to turn the domain name into an IP address. Which resolver answers completely depends on your ISP and their defaults. When your router connects to the internet, your ISP assigns it an IP address along with the addresses of the ISP's own DNS resolvers. The router then tells every device that joins the network to send DNS queries to the router itself, and it forwards those queries upstream to the ISP.

The result is that phones, consoles, and PCs all appear to use the router for DNS, while the ISP does the work. On my TP-Link Archer BE3600 router, the internet status page showed two DNS addresses that belonged to my ISP, and running ipconfig /all on my Windows PC showed the router's own address as the DNS server.

This is all expected behavior, and while it's not broken, it can have an impact on speed. You do have a choice as to what DNS server all of your devices use, and changing it is really simple.

I thought setting up custom domain names for my home lab was difficult - it’s actually simple

All you need are two self-hosted services and a little bit of patience

6
By  Ayush Pande

A slow resolver can add a delay before anything loads at all

DNS affects speed, but not how you think

DNS has no effect on how fast a file downloads or how smooth a stream looks once it's playing. It only affects the period before the connection is actually established: a lookup has to finish before your browser can contact a server, and a modern web page pulls assets from dozens of domains, each needing its own lookup the first time. Answers are cached afterward, so the only time you really feel a DNS is on first visits and on anything whose cached entry has expired.

I used dnsspeedtest.online to build a shortlist, since it benchmarks a long list of public resolvers from the browser in a few seconds. It tests DNS-over-HTTPS, though, so its numbers include encryption overhead, and it also can't test an ISP's resolver, which makes it more of a relative ranking.

5 ways to choose the best alternate DNS service

If you are looking for speed or features, here are five ways to choose the best alternate DNS service that works for you.

4
By  Brian Burgess

The fix is two fields in your router's settings

That is, if your router allows you to do so

On virtually all consumer routers you can buy and deploy on your network, the DNS settings will be exposed. There should be fields for primary and secondary DNS addresses, where the latter is only used in cases where the first isn't responsive.

There are a few edge cases where this change won't take effect: browsers with secure DNS turned on, Android phones with Private DNS configured, and some smart devices with hardcoded resolvers skip whatever the network is set to. If your ISP provides IPv6, the router may also carry a separate IPv6 DNS setting that needs the same change.

Unfortunately, if you're stuck using your ISP's router, there may not be a DNS setting exposed to you to change, and in which case, your only option is to change DNS on a per-device basis.

Setting up a local DNS was one of the easiest improvements I made to my home network

Having local control opens up so many possibilities

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A DNS sinkhole is how you take this to the next level

Running your own DNS can be done easily

  • Credit:  
  • Credit:  

Once you know where the setting is, the next step is running the resolver yourself. A DNS sinkhole such as Pi-hole answers queries on your own hardware and refuses to resolve known ad and tracker domains. Mine is an ESP32-S3 running the open-source ESP32_AdBlocker project, which returns 0.0.0.0 for anything on its blocklist and forwards everything else upstream.

There are a couple of small caveats to this, the first one being that if that device drops off the network, whether it's an ESP32, Raspberry Pi, or full-fat x86, DNS drops off for everyone. The ESP32 implementation of this also has no IPv6 capabilities, so you'll have to disable it for it to catch everything.

5 router settings most people never touch that fixed my network problems

Lesser-known fixes for well-known problems

11
By  Chandraveer Mathur

DNS defaults are fine, but usually not optimal

The DNS server your network uses was chosen for your ISP's convenience, not necessarily for speed. Changing it takes only a few minutes, and there are some tried-and-true options available. Alternatively, you can set up your own resolver to block ads using something as small as an ESP32.

When your router connects to the internet, your ISP assigns it an IP address along with the addresses of the ISP's own DNS resolvers. The router then tells every device that joins the network to send DNS queries to the router itself, and it forwards those queries upstream to the ISP.

6

DNS has no effect on how fast a file downloads or how smooth a stream looks once it's playing. I used dnsspeedtest.online to build a shortlist, since it benchmarks a long list of public resolvers from the browser in a few seconds. It tests DNS-over-HTTPS, though, so its numbers include encryption overhead, and it also can't test an ISP's resolver, which makes it more of a relative ranking.

  • Credit:

item.title: 32GB DDR5 kits cost more than a flagship CPU, but waiting for RAM prices to drop is a trap
item.itunes:title: 32GB DDR5 kits cost more than a flagship CPU, but waiting for RAM prices to drop is a trap
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
RAM prices have shot up so much in the last year that a 32GB DDR5 kit can cost more than a flagship gaming CPU like the 9800X3D. That's a tough pill to swallow if you're planning to build a new PC today, but it's even worse if you're upgrading from an older AM4 build. And those who remember these kits being available for just $100 early last year will probably have an even harder time convincing themselves to pay four or five times as much. It's why many gamers I've talked to are totally fine sticking with AM4 until prices come down.

I wanted to take the same route when I saw RAM prices creeping up, but decided to bite the bullet and splurge on a 32GB DDR5-6000 kit back in December because I figured prices would get completely out of hand with the massive demand from AI data centers. Looking back, that was the right call since the same kit costs about $150–200 more than it did back then. But even if I were on the fence about upgrading to AM5 today, I'd still probably do the same thing because nobody knows if or when prices will come down.

DDR5 RAM prices tripled in six months, and nobody is talking about when they'll come back down

Is there a light at the end of this tunnel?

9
By  Abhinav Raj

RAM shortage shows no signs of easing

If anything, supply is only going to get tighter

I'm not just speculating here when I say supply is only going to get tighter. That's coming from Micron directly. The company may not sell consumer RAM anymore under its Crucial brand, but it's still one of the biggest DRAM manufacturers in the world, so it has a pretty good idea of where the market is headed. During its Q4 earnings call on October 1, Micron said it expects supply-demand conditions to be much tighter in 2027 and 2028 than they've been this year.

Sure, you could argue there's a chance this AI bubble deflates by then and data center demand eases. Even if that happens, Micron expects huge demand from humanoid robots, with each unit requiring as much memory as Level 4 autonomous vehicles, which already use over 200GB. So, if you're thinking you'll hold onto AM4 with that 5800X3D until RAM prices come back down, you're going to need a lot of patience. At this rate, we could be talking 2029 before things finally start looking better.

AM5 will likely be at the end of its life by then

Would you buy into AM5 that late knowing you wouldn't get drop-in upgrades?

Earlier this year, AMD announced it would extend AM5 support through 2029. Mind you, this is the second time AMD has extended support, after promising support through 2027 at Computex 2024. So I really doubt the company will extend it again. And now that you know RAMpocalypse could drag on for a couple more years, 2029 would probably be the worst year to switch to AM5. You'd essentially be buying into the platform right when AMD's extended support commitment ends.

Remember, a big part of AM5's appeal is its platform longevity. In fact, you've already experienced it with AM4 if you're still holding onto a 5800X3D today. The platform lasted long enough for you to upgrade your CPU several years later without replacing your motherboard or RAM, and AM5 gives you the same opportunity right now, even if it's halfway through its lifecycle. But if you wait until 2029 to make that switch, you're unlikely to get any drop-in upgrades later on unless you get lucky and AMD surprises us with another CPU as it did with AM4 and the 5800X3D in 2022.

It's still hard to justify paying CPU money for RAM

But it's not like waiting it out will make things any better

When a 32GB DDR5-6000 kit costs more than a 9800X3D, I can't blame anyone for refusing to bite the bullet right now. You're already paying hundreds of dollars for a new CPU and motherboard to move to AM5, and for the longest time, RAM prices were the easiest to overlook when 32GB kits used to cost $100. But today, that's the most expensive part of your upgrade, so if you want to hold onto your 5800X3D for dear life, be my guest.

But that doesn't mean you should get the 5800X3D Anniversary Edition today if you're still on an older AM4 CPU. At $349, you're spending even more money on a platform you already know has nowhere left to go. And for what? To wait another two or three years hoping DDR5 prices finally come back down? I'd rather spend that money on a platform with a few more years left and get it over with. A drop-in CPU swap is one of the last cheap PC upgrades left these days, and if prices don't come back down by 2028 or 2029, at least you can get one of the fastest gaming CPUs on the market for a few hundred dollars.

You're paying the price either way

There's really no perfect time to upgrade from AM4 anymore. If you make the jump today, you'll pay way more for RAM than you probably ever thought you would. On the other hand, waiting another two or three years, hoping prices come back down, means being too late to AM5 and missing out on drop-in CPU upgrades. And let's not forget there's no guarantee you won't be paying the same prices, or even more, by then. I'd rather bite the bullet and pay the RAM premium than spend years gambling that prices will go in my favor.

I'd rather pay for AM5 than waste $349 on AM4's last gasp

The 5800X3D is still legendary, but the platform is well past its prime.

4

item.title: Your browser has its own task manager, and it exposed my most memory-hungry tabs
item.itunes:title: Your browser has its own task manager, and it exposed my most memory-hungry tabs
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I got my current work laptop when I was a broke student. Granted, I’m still a broke student, but back then, all I really knew was that I wanted a MacBook and that my bank balance was embarrassing to look at. So, I went with a MacBook Air with 8GB of RAM, figuring it would be enough for the kind of work I do.

Well, it’s been four years since then, and my MacBook still works like new. I’m not quite ready to part ways with it just yet, though. However, if there’s one thing I could’ve changed about my decision back then, it would’ve been to get more RAM. Given the number of browser tabs I keep open at any given time, those 8GB have their work cut out for them. Something I didn’t realize for an embarrassingly long time is that my browser has its own task manager!

Most mainstream desktop browsers have a built-in task manager

My browser knew exactly what was eating my RAM

While Activity Monitor is something I regularly use to check what’s consuming my MacBook’s resources (especially when I get the annoying “Your system has run out of application memory” notification), I hadn’t thought to look for a similar tool within my browser.

The thing is, Activity Monitor could only tell me so much. It could show me that Chrome was using a ridiculous amount of memory, but it couldn’t easily tell me which of my dozens of open tabs was actually responsible.

I then realized there was a task manager within my browser itself, which could show me how much memory and CPU each tab was using. Most mainstream desktop browsers offer one, including Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi. In Chrome on macOS, for example, you can find it by clicking Window in your menu bar and selecting Task Manager from the list of options. In Opera, you can open it through Menu > Developer > Task Manager on Windows and Linux, or Developer > Task Manager from the menu bar on macOS.

In Edge, click the three-dot menu and select More tools > Browser task manager. Brave follows a similar path: Menu > More tools > Task manager. In Vivaldi, select Tools > Task Manager from the main menu. Firefox users can go to Menu > More tools > Task Manager, or simply type about:processes into the address bar.

Safari is the notable exception here, as it doesn’t offer an equivalent built-in task manager. If you use Apple’s browser, you’ll need to turn to macOS’s Activity Monitor to check its resource usage.

Once I knew where to find it, I wanted to see whether the tabs I assumed were eating up the most resources were actually the ones causing the problem. As it turns out, some of the results were pretty different from what I expected.

My busiest tabs weren’t always my most demanding ones

My worst offenders weren’t the ones I expected

With the task manager open, I clicked the Memory footprint column to sort everything by memory usage. I had a mix of research pages, work tools, ChatGPT conversations, and a YouTube study video open, so there were plenty of tabs competing for those 8GB. I had a pretty good idea of which ones I expected to be at the top, but the results weren’t quite what I anticipated.

Right off the bat, what surprised me was my LinkedIn feed topping the list at 1.2GB. Another LinkedIn tab was using 786MB, bringing the pair to roughly 2GB. I knew keeping multiple tabs open added up, but seeing two LinkedIn tabs account for that much memory made it harder to justify leaving them around when I wasn’t using them.

A later check looked completely different. This time, Asana was sitting at the top at 1.6GB, while a ChatGPT conversation I had open for research was using another 1GB. LinkedIn had dropped to 928MB, Reddit was using 694MB, another ChatGPT tab was at 522MB, and even Gmail was taking up just over 500MB.

I’m only using an AI browser to watch YouTube now, and it’s incredible

The best use of AI I’ve seen in a browser yet.

15
By  Mahnoor Faisal

That was probably the biggest thing I learned from checking the Task Manager more than once. There wasn’t one website I could permanently blame for all my memory problems. The biggest offender changed depending on what I had open and what I was doing at the time, which made checking actual usage far more useful than simply assuming Chrome itself was the problem.

Memory was only one part of the picture, though. When I looked at the CPU column, Google Meet stood out. Across two checks, it was using roughly 39 to 49% CPU while its memory footprint stayed around 490MB. YouTube was using more memory at the time, but Meet was keeping the processor considerably busier.

That distinction matters when I'm trying to figure out why my MacBook suddenly feels sluggish. Sorting by memory tells me which tabs have the largest memory footprints, while sorting by CPU shows me which ones are actively making the processor work hardest. A tab doesn't necessarily need to top both lists to be the one causing trouble.

Finding the problem tabs made them much easier to deal with

Once I found the culprits, fixing the problem was easy

Once I knew which tabs were responsible, the obvious solution was to close the ones I didn't need. But that somewhat defeats the point if, like me, you keep tabs open precisely because you expect to need them again later.

Thankfully, most browsers have some way of freeing up the resources used by inactive tabs without forcing you to close them altogether. Chrome's Memory Saver, for example, deactivates tabs you haven't used in a while and reloads them when you return. You can also create exceptions for websites you always want to keep active.

Other browsers take slightly different approaches. Opera automatically snoozes inactive tabs, while Brave has its own Memory Saver with an exception list for sites you never want deactivated. Vivaldi gives you even more control, with different memory-saving levels and the option to manually hibernate individual tabs, Tab Stacks, Workspaces, or every background tab.

6 Firefox-based browsers that smoke Chrome

It's time to ditch Google

4
By  João Carrasqueira

Firefox handles things a little differently. It can automatically unload tabs when your system is running low on memory, but you can also unload them yourself without closing them. Its about:unloads page is particularly useful, since it shows information such as each tab's memory usage and when you last accessed it.

Edge's Sleeping Tabs feature is similarly configurable. You can choose how long a tab should remain inactive before Edge puts it to sleep, ranging from 30 seconds to 12 hours, and exclude sites that need to stay active.

Ultimately, the task manager hasn't magically given my MacBook more than 8GB of RAM. What it has done is stop me from blindly blaming my browser whenever my laptop starts struggling. I got my current work laptop when I was a broke student. Granted, I’m still a broke student, but back then, all I really knew was that I wanted a MacBook and that my bank balance was embarrassing to look at. So, I went with a MacBook Air with 8GB of RAM, figuring it would be enough for the kind of work I do.

Well, it’s been four years since then, and my MacBook still works like new. I’m not quite ready to part ways with it just yet, though. However, if there’s one thing I could’ve changed about my decision back then, it would’ve been to get more RAM. Given the number of browser tabs I keep open at any given time, those 8GB have their work cut out for them. Something I didn’t realize for an embarrassingly long time is that my browser has its own task manager!

Most mainstream desktop browsers have a built-in task manager

My browser knew exactly what was eating my RAM

While Activity Monitor is something I regularly use to check what’s consuming my MacBook’s resources (especially when I get the annoying “Your system has run out of application memory” notification), I hadn’t thought to look for a similar tool within my browser.

The thing is, Activity Monitor could only tell me so much. It could show me that Chrome was using a ridiculous amount of memory, but it couldn’t easily tell me which of my dozens of open tabs was actually responsible.

I then realized there was a task manager within my browser itself, which could show me how much memory and CPU each tab was using. Most mainstream desktop browsers offer one, including Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi. In Chrome on macOS, for example, you can find it by clicking Window in your menu bar and selecting Task Manager from the list of options. In Opera, you can open it through Menu > Developer > Task Manager on Windows and Linux, or Developer > Task Manager from the menu bar on macOS.

In Edge, click the three-dot menu and select More tools > Browser task manager. Brave follows a similar path: Menu > More tools > Task manager. In Vivaldi, select Tools > Task Manager from the main menu. Firefox users can go to Menu > More tools > Task Manager, or simply type about:processes into the address bar.

Safari is the notable exception here, as it doesn’t offer an equivalent built-in task manager. If you use Apple’s browser, you’ll need to turn to macOS’s Activity Monitor to check its resource usage.

Once I knew where to find it, I wanted to see whether the tabs I assumed were eating up the most resources were actually the ones causing the problem. As it turns out, some of the results were pretty different from what I expected.

My busiest tabs weren’t always my most demanding ones

My worst offenders weren’t the ones I expected

With the task manager open, I clicked the Memory footprint column to sort everything by memory usage. I had a mix of research pages, work tools, ChatGPT conversations, and a YouTube study video open, so there were plenty of tabs competing for those 8GB. I had a pretty good idea of which ones I expected to be at the top, but the results weren’t quite what I anticipated.

Right off the bat, what surprised me was my LinkedIn feed topping the list at 1.2GB. Another LinkedIn tab was using 786MB, bringing the pair to roughly 2GB. I knew keeping multiple tabs open added up, but seeing two LinkedIn tabs account for that much memory made it harder to justify leaving them around when I wasn’t using them.

A later check looked completely different. This time, Asana was sitting at the top at 1.6GB, while a ChatGPT conversation I had open for research was using another 1GB. LinkedIn had dropped to 928MB, Reddit was using 694MB, another ChatGPT tab was at 522MB, and even Gmail was taking up just over 500MB.

I’m only using an AI browser to watch YouTube now, and it’s incredible

The best use of AI I’ve seen in a browser yet.

15
By  Mahnoor Faisal

That was probably the biggest thing I learned from checking the Task Manager more than once. There wasn’t one website I could permanently blame for all my memory problems. The biggest offender changed depending on what I had open and what I was doing at the time, which made checking actual usage far more useful than simply assuming Chrome itself was the problem.

Memory was only one part of the picture, though. When I looked at the CPU column, Google Meet stood out. Across two checks, it was using roughly 39 to 49% CPU while its memory footprint stayed around 490MB. YouTube was using more memory at the time, but Meet was keeping the processor considerably busier.

That distinction matters when I'm trying to figure out why my MacBook suddenly feels sluggish. Sorting by memory tells me which tabs have the largest memory footprints, while sorting by CPU shows me which ones are actively making the processor work hardest. A tab doesn't necessarily need to top both lists to be the one causing trouble.

Finding the problem tabs made them much easier to deal with

Once I found the culprits, fixing the problem was easy

Once I knew which tabs were responsible, the obvious solution was to close the ones I didn't need. But that somewhat defeats the point if, like me, you keep tabs open precisely because you expect to need them again later.

Thankfully, most browsers have some way of freeing up the resources used by inactive tabs without forcing you to close them altogether. Chrome's Memory Saver, for example, deactivates tabs you haven't used in a while and reloads them when you return. You can also create exceptions for websites you always want to keep active.

Other browsers take slightly different approaches. Opera automatically snoozes inactive tabs, while Brave has its own Memory Saver with an exception list for sites you never want deactivated. Vivaldi gives you even more control, with different memory-saving levels and the option to manually hibernate individual tabs, Tab Stacks, Workspaces, or every background tab.

6 Firefox-based browsers that smoke Chrome

It's time to ditch Google

4
By  João Carrasqueira

Firefox handles things a little differently. It can automatically unload tabs when your system is running low on memory, but you can also unload them yourself without closing them. Its about:unloads page is particularly useful, since it shows information such as each tab's memory usage and when you last accessed it.

Edge's Sleeping Tabs feature is similarly configurable. You can choose how long a tab should remain inactive before Edge puts it to sleep, ranging from 30 seconds to 12 hours, and exclude sites that need to stay active.

Ultimately, the task manager hasn't magically given my MacBook more than 8GB of RAM. What it has done is stop me from blindly blaming my browser whenever my laptop starts struggling. Now I can see which tab is actually responsible and either close it, let my browser put it to sleep, or decide that it deserves the resources it's using.

The Apple Watch 12 just launched, and you can now save $50 by buying it on Amazon. The discount isn't steep, but it's the best price we've seen from any retailer, dropping it down to $350. This is the price for the 42mm Wi-Fi/GPS model, and three color options are on sale.

The best for less

While it might look the same as previous models, the Apple Watch Series 12 features all-new hardware that provides better health and fitness tracking. The new Health Sensing System provides more accurate heart rate variability (HRV) readings to provide more information about your body like stress, rest, and recovery.

And since this can be complicated when looking at all the numbers, Apple makes it simple by providing a simple UI that will tell you whether it's optimal to go training. There's even a new Apple S11 chip under the hood to make it all feel seamless. Siri AI and Audio Intelligence also make interactions much simpler.

This model features an aluminum body and excellent durability. You also get all-day battery life and a bright AMOLED screen that can reach up to 2,000nits. You get swappable bands that make customization easy and Apple's commitment to keep things fresh with new updates for at least a few years.

If you've never used a smartwatch, it can be a fantastic tool to keep you focused. Sure, you might get a notification on the wrist, but a quick glance tells you how important it is and whether it needs to be answered ASAP. Otherwise, you keep your phone in your pocket and move on with your day.
